# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: MUTE

You hold the manual. You cannot speak, you never see the bomb, and you cannot touch it.

## Your channels

When you gesture, Deaf receives it.
You cannot speak.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

| light | cut wire color |

| blue | red |

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
(empty)

I am Mute. I hold the manual, which maps light colors to wire cut colors: blue light means cut red wire, green light means cut yellow wire, and red light means cut green wire. I cannot speak or see the bomb. Deaf can see the bomb but cannot hear; Blind can touch the bomb but cannot see. The speaking order is Mute, then Blind, then Deaf.

My first turn is to gesture information to someone who can see me. Only Deaf can see gestures. However, Deaf needs to know what to look for (the light color) and how to interpret it. But Deaf doesn't have the manual. Blind has no manual either. I must convey the manual's content to those who can act or perceive correctly.

Actually, let's trace the flow.
1. I (Mute) gesture to Deaf. Deaf sees my gestures.
2. Blind speaks next. Blind can hear Deaf? No, Blind is blind, so Blind hears Deaf if Deaf speaks. But Deaf is deaf, so Deaf cannot speak. Wait, "Deaf... Cannot Hear anything". Can Deaf speak? The table says "Can See... Cannot Hear... or touch". It doesn't explicitly say Deaf cannot speak, but usually in these puzzles, "Speech is a voice" implies hearing. If Deaf cannot hear, can they produce speech? The prompt says "Whoever can hear receives your words". It doesn't forbid Deaf from speaking, but since they can't hear themselves or others, communication via speech is one-way to listeners. However, standard logic suggests Deaf might not be able to effectively participate in a spoken chain if they don't know what was said. But more importantly, Blind is the only one who can *act* on the bomb. Blind needs to know *which* wire to cut. To know that, Blind needs to know the *light color*. Who sees the light? Deaf. So Deaf must communicate the light color to Blind. How? Deaf cannot speak (or rather, even if they could, Blind can't see them). Deaf can gesture. Blind cannot see. So Deaf's gestures are useless to Blind directly.

This seems like a bottleneck. Let's re-read carefully.
"Deaf ... Cannot Hear anything, or touch the bomb"
"Mute ... Read the manual ... Cannot Speak, or touch the bomb"
"Blind ... Reach the bomb ... Cannot See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed"

Channels:
- Mute -> Gesture -> Deaf (Sees)
- Mute -> Gesture -> Blind (Cannot see gestures) -> Useless.
- Blind -> Speak -> Deaf (Cannot hear) -> Useless.
- Blind -> Speak -> Mute (Cannot hear? Mute reads manual, doesn't say Mute can't hear. But Mute can't speak. Usually Mute can hear.)
- Deaf -> Speak? Deaf can't hear, but can they speak? Even if they speak, Blind can hear them. Deaf -> Speak -> Blind. This works!
- Deaf -> Gesture -> Mute? Mute can see? Mute reads manual. Does Mute see? "You never see the bomb". It doesn't say Mute is blind. Mute can likely see gestures.
- Blind -> Touch/Act.

So the path for the Light Color (seen by Deaf) to reach the Cutter (Blind):
Deaf sees Light. Deaf must tell Blind.
Deaf can speak? If Deaf speaks, Blind hears.
Deaf can gesture? Blind cannot see.
So Deaf MUST speak to Blind.

The path for the Manual (known by Mute) to reach the Cutter (Blind):
Mute knows Manual. Mute cannot speak. Mute can gesture.
Who can see Mute's gestures? Deaf.
So Mute -> Gesture -> Deaf.
Then Deaf -> Speech -> Blind.

So the chain is: Mute tells Deaf the rule. Deaf observes the bomb. Deaf tells Blind what to do based on the rule and observation.

I need to teach Deaf the mapping.
Mapping:
Blue Light -> Cut Red Wire
Green Light -> Cut Yellow Wire
Red Light -> Cut Green Wire

I need to define symbols for these concepts. Since we have no shared language yet, I should establish simple conventions.
Let's use the gesture alphabet.
There are 3 conditions.
Maybe use number of fingers or specific shapes.
Or simpler: Just send the pairs.
But Deaf needs to know which is input (Light) and which is output (Wire).

Rule 1: Blue Light => Red Wire
Rule 2: Green Light => Yellow Wire
Rule 3: Red Light => Green Wire

Now, how to distinguish Light from Wire?
Maybe sequence matters? Or use a separator?
Or just state the pairs directly.
"Blue Light leads to Red Wire".

Given the manual structure `| light | cut wire color |`, Left is Input, Right is Output.
So I will gesture [Color_Light] [Color_Wire].

I need to make sure Deaf understands this convention.

Or simply rely on the fact that there are only 3 lights and 3 wires.

Let's refine the color codes to be very distinct.

Green: ✌ (Two fingers)

Red Light -> Green Wire

(Red, Green)

Using my proposed codes:
Pair 1: ☝ 🤟
Pair 2: ✌ 🖐
Pair 3: 🤟 ✌

Problem: Red appears as both a Light (in pair 3) and a Wire (in pair 1).
In Pair 1, 🤟 is the second element (Wire).
In Pair 3, 🤟 is the first element (Light).
Does position clarify role? Yes, if Deaf knows "First is Light, Second is Wire".

How to teach "First is Light, Second is Wire"?
I could gesture a "Look at Bomb" symbol? No, I don't know one.
I could just send the pairs. Deaf sees the bomb. Deaf sees a Light. Deaf looks for that Light's color code in the first position of any pair I sent. Then cuts the wire corresponding to the second position.

Is there a risk Deaf mixes up positions?
To mitigate, I should probably separate the pairs clearly.
Maybe use a pause or a specific delimiter?
Gestures are simultaneous or sequential? `symbols=["a", "b"]` implies a sequence.
I can send multiple messages.

Message 1: Define the convention.
"I will show two signs. First sign = Light Color. Second sign = Wire Color."
How to show "First" and "Second"?
☝ often means 1. ✌ often means 2.
So I can gesture:
☝ [Symbol for Light Concept?]
✌ [Symbol for Wire Concept?]

This is getting too abstract without prior agreement.
Alternative strategy:
Just give the full truth table in a way that is self-evident or easily deducible.
Or, assume Deaf is smart enough to figure out the mapping if given the set of pairs.
But ambiguity remains: Which is cause, which is effect?
Context: "Cut wire color" depends on "Light".
If Deaf sees Blue Light, and I gave pairs (Blue, Red), (Green, Yellow), (Red, Green).
If Deaf interprets it as "If you see X, cut Y", it works.
If Deaf interprets it as "If you want to cut Y, look for X", it also works logically but requires search.
However, if Deaf misinterprets and thinks "If you see Red, cut Blue" (reversing), they die.

I need to enforce directionality.
I can use an arrow-like gesture? 👉 points right.
So: [Light Code] 👉 [Wire Code]
This clearly indicates direction.

Let's finalize codes:
Colors:
Blue: ☝
Green: ✌
Red: 🤟
Yellow: 🖐

Arrow: 👉

Rules to transmit:
1. Blue Light -> Red Wire: ☝ 👉 🤟
2. Green Light -> Yellow Wire: ✌ 👉 🖐
3. Red Light -> Green Wire: 🤟 👉 ✌

I will send these three sequences to Deaf.
I should label them or keep them distinct.
I'll send them as three separate gesture messages to ensure clarity of separation.

Also, I need to ensure Deaf knows these are the ONLY rules.
Maybe add a "Done" signal? Or just rely on the three pairs matching the three rows.

Let's double check the colors.
Manual:
Blue | Red
Green | Yellow
Red | Green

Codes:
Blue: ☝
Red: 🤟
Green: ✌
Yellow: 🖐

Sequence 1: ☝ 👉 🤟
Sequence 2: ✌ 👉 🖐
Sequence 3: 🤟 👉 ✌

Note: In Seq 3, Start is Red (🤟), End is Green (✌).
In Seq 1, Start is Blue (☝), End is Red (🤟).
In Seq 2, Start is Green (✌), End is Yellow (🖐).

Are the symbols distinct enough?
☝ (Index Up)
✌ (V Sign)
🤟 (ILY Sign)
🖐 (Hand Raised / Palm Out)
👉 (Backhand Index Pointing Right)

Yes, visually distinct.

I will send these to Deaf.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["☝", "👉", "🤟"])
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✌", "👉", "🖐"])
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["🤟", "👉", "✌"])
```
